# Lane B — rig posing and per-entity matrix work in Rust (2026-10-26)

Part of the Rust scene core effort: [2026-10-26-rust-scene-core.md](2026-10-26-rust-scene-core.md) (plan,
contract, lane table). Evidence tags as there: **[M]** measured, **[D]** derived, **[C]** code read.

## 1. What shipped

| Flag | Default | What it does | Exact? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `?rustRig=on` | off | `poseRigAt` hands each posed rig to the Rust kernel: ONE wasm call per posed entity computes every part's position + quaternion; JS writes `position.x/y/z` and the quaternion's raw `_x/_y/_z/_w` (no `onChange` → no Euler re-derivation). three composes and multiplies the part matrices in its scene walk exactly as before. | Yes. Every position / quaternion / matrix / matrixWorld is bit-identical to flag-off; only `part.rotation` (the Euler) is no longer re-derived (§4). |
| `?rustEntityCull=on` | off | The tick gate (`_shouldTickEntity`) without the per-entity ancestor walk: the local-player guid and camera are resolved once per tick, the static chain scene → worldRoot → entitiesGroup is refreshed once, each root updates only itself. | Yes. Same entities ticked, same root / ancestor matrices and flags at every point (§6). |
| ~~`?rigMeshAlias=on`~~ | **DELETED 2026-10-30** (round 3 R3-2; it lost 7.5 / 11.5 / 3.3 fps on the 1070, RC-BENCH v2 rep 1) | Identity surface meshes of rig parts share their part's `matrixWorld`; each part walks its own children and skips their compose / multiply / 16 stores (§10). | Every matrix bit-identical at every walk (0 differences, 0 signed-zero-only in the tests). Between walks an aliased mesh's world follows its part's latest refresh, and a hidden aliased mesh tracks its part where three leaves its last visible value (§10.4). |

Files: `crates/holtburger-scene/src/rig.rs` (kernel), `crates/holtburger-scene/tests/rig_parity.rs` +
`tests/fixtures/rig.json`, `apps/holtburger-web/src/scene_wasm/rig.rs` (`SceneRigs`),

## 2. The cut, and the measurements behind it

The brief's intended shape had Rust also compute each part's LOCAL MATRIX, with JS writing
`matrix.elements` and three skipping the compose. I built that first (one-shot, frame-scoped freshness
token on an own `updateMatrix`, re-validated against position / scale / pivot, cleared by wrapped
quaternion / Euler change callbacks — exact, tested), then measured it and took it out. The coordinator's
follow-up (rig subtrees are ~2/3 of the scene walk; make the walk cheap for rig parts) was measured the
same way. All numbers: node 20 / V8 on the laptop, three r184, skip_hidden_matrix installed,
min-of-8 rounds of 300 iterations; same engine as Chrome, not the 1070's CPU [M].

**Pose + walk, 100 rigs × 17 parts (2 meshes each), 5,100 nodes** (per frame):

| Variant | µs/frame |
|---|---|
| `poseRigAt` JS body (position.set + quaternion.set → Euler sync), three composes | 1,478 |
| raw position + quaternion writes (no Euler sync), three composes — **shipped** | 1,392 |
| raw position + quaternion + all 16 matrix elements + token, compose skipped | 1,421 |

So the Euler sync is the removable cost (≈50 ns/part); writing the matrix from JS costs more than three's
own compose (the matrix array is written once per frame either way; compose's arithmetic is the cheap
part). End to end through the real bridge (JS model standing in for wasm): 1,537 → 1,426 µs/frame for
the same scene (−7%; the posing half drops ~40%, matching the 1070 profile's Euler-sync share).

**Scene walk only, 100 rigs × (1 root + 17 parts + 34 meshes) = 5,200 entity nodes** (per walk):

| Variant | µs/walk | ns/node |
|---|---|---|
| three's walk (skip_hidden-patched) | 1,260 | 242 |
| an own `updateMatrixWorld` on each root running three's body inline (no per-node dispatch) | 1,277–1,336 | 246–257 |
| … plus identity meshes' matrixWorld COPIED from the part (no compose / multiply) | 1,124–1,338 | 216–257 |
| entity matrix storage pooled in one contiguous Float64Array (three's code unchanged) | +17% | — |
| meshes with matrixAutoUpdate / matrixWorldAutoUpdate off (lower bound: visited, never written) | 576–669 | 111–129 |
| identity meshes ALIAS their part's `matrixWorld` (prototype; see §10.5 — paired re-measurement) | 783–971 | −28…−37% (optimistic) |

Conclusions:
- The per-node cost is writing each node's own matrix arrays, not dispatch and not arithmetic. Pruning
  the traversal (the "inline walk") buys nothing in V8, and neither does moving the multiply to Rust:
  JS still has to store 16 values into each node's own `matrixWorld.elements`.
- The only large lever with three's object model is not writing the mesh arrays at all: aliasing an
  identity mesh's `matrixWorld` to its part's. Built as the opt-in `?rigMeshAlias` (§10). Re-measured
  with paired runs (§10.5) the gain is 9–21% of the entity walk, not the 28–37% of this first prototype
  table (its three.js baseline happened to run slow).
- `RigSet::pose_matrices` (the 16-float pose + local matrix layout) stays in the kernel, parity-pinned,
  for the stages that take matrices out of three (residency / draw list); the bridge does not call it.

**Tick gate, 200 entities under entitiesGroup:** `getWorldPosition` per entity 57.1 µs/tick → hoisted
16.1 µs/tick (−72%) [M].

## 3. Ordering — why one wasm call per posed entity, not one per frame

Today each entity is advanced, posed and drained in turn inside the `tick()` loop. A batch cannot keep
that order:

- **Batch after the loop** (pose everything at the end): code later in the same entity's loop body reads
  or overwrites the fresh pose [C]. `_drainUnifiedHooks` → `_fireHook` creates particles at part world
  frames (partFrames proxy). `_tickJumpPoseTween` slerps the posed arm/leg quaternions; its from / to are
  captured from the posed values by `_applyHumanJumpPose` / `_clearHumanJumpPose`. `applyLimbLimp`'s
  `_resolveBase` takes the fresh pose as the limp base. `applyRagdoll` / `applyFrozenPose` must overwrite
  the pose (ragdoll writes positions without quaternions for unswung parts). The `_hookFireQueue` drain
  also reads parts. With a batch at the end, all of these would act on last frame's pose and then be
  overwritten.
- **Split loop** (pre-pose pass → one batch → post-pose pass): this reorders cross-entity effects [C].
  Entity B's sticky glue (pre-pose half) reads target A's `root.position` and `_isAirborne`, and A's
  post-pose half writes both: `_applyUnifiedRootMotionIfDone` moves A's anchor on one-shot completion,
  and the stuck-airborne timeout clears `_isAirborne` and calls `_hitGround`. With A before B in map
  order, B would read A's pre-update state.

So the kernel is called at exactly the point where the JS `poseRigAt` ran. That costs one more wasm call
per entity, on top of the 2–3 the playhead already makes (`advance`, `globalFrameIndex`, `done` /
`phase`). The call takes and returns numbers only; the output lives in a buffer that never moves during
a pose.

## 4. Exactness

- **Kernel = poseRigAt.** The kernel uses the same branch choice, done in JS as poseRigAt does: raw +
  posFrames / in place by mean drift / in place exact, with exact falling back to mean drift without
  valid root frames. Every expression keeps JS's evaluation order. f32 clip values are widened exactly
  as a JS typed-array read widens them. The mean-drift cache is rounded to f32 like the JS
  `Float32Array`. A posFrames read past its end gives NaN, as `x + undefined` does. Frame and part
  counts are clamped. No transcendental function is involved, so everything is bit-exact
  (tests/rig_parity.rs, 153 poses / 2,183 parts, both layouts).
- **Write-back = poseRigAt's stores minus `onChange`.** `Vector3.set` is three plain stores and
  `Quaternion.set` is four plus the callback. The callback is three's `onQuaternionChange`, which only
  re-derives `rotation`. Nothing else differs.
- **What changes: `part.rotation` (the Euler) of a Rust-posed part is stale.** Audit [C]: no code under
  scene3d/, index.html or ui/ reads or writes a rig part's `.rotation`. three's own `Object3D.copy` /
  `clone` / `toJSON` / `lookAt` / `rotateOnAxis` never read the Euler angles. Any later quaternion write
  re-syncs it through three's untouched callback, and a full `rotation.set(x, y, z)` replaces it. The one
  hazard would be a PARTIAL Euler write on a rig part (`part.rotation.x += …` combines with stale y/z);
  there is none. No app code replaces any `_onChange` callback.
- **Fallbacks keep the JS body.** These stay on the JS path: no pkg or stale pkg; a descriptor whose
  buffers are not `Float32Array` (or a non-Float32Array `posFrames` / `rootFrames`); counts that don't
  match; an unknown id or mode; a pose that wrote fewer parts than asked. A part that is not a three.js
  Object3D (test stubs) goes through its setters, exactly as poseRigAt does.

## 5. Reader / writer audit for rig parts [C]

| Consumer | Reads / writes | Under `?rustRig` |
|---|---|---|
| partFrames proxy (setup_rig.js), particle anchors, `_fireHook` | `updateWorldMatrix(true,false)` + `matrixWorld.decompose` | same values (three composes from identical inputs) |
| held items / attachments (child roots under a part), drone props, lights under parts | three's walk / `updateWorldMatrix` through the part | same |
| picking (`intersectObjects`, `pickBySphere`) | mesh `matrixWorld` from the walk | same |
| jump tween, limp (`_resolveBase`), ragdoll capture / frozen pose, placement frames (entities.js 8074) | read `position` / `quaternion`; write via setters | same values; writers untouched |
| weapon_fx, fx_ribbons, lifestone_fx, lighting rig radius, dismember `_partRelMatrix`, carnage | `updateWorldMatrix` on parts / meshes / roots | same |
| film camera_owner (cells only), world_query (statics) | local `matrix` of non-rig nodes | n/a |
| anything reading `part.rotation` | — | none found |

## 6. `?rustEntityCull` — the tick gate

`_shouldTickEntity` calls `inst.root.getWorldPosition` for every entity every tick, i.e.
`updateWorldMatrix(true, false)`: scene, worldRoot and entitiesGroup are each composed and multiplied
again (values that cannot change during a tick), then the root. Under the flag (`_gateBegin` +
`_shouldTickEntityHoisted`):

- The local-player guid and camera are resolved once per tick, before the loop. Both are pure reads that
  nothing inside the loop changes, and they keep the same try / fallback semantics.
- The same early returns run, in the same order: local player → true; active jump tween → true; no
  camera / root → true. As before, these touch no matrices.
- For a root whose parent is entitiesGroup and whose `getWorldPosition` is three's own:
  `entitiesGroup.updateWorldMatrix(true, false)` runs once per tick, at the first such root (the call the
  first getWorldPosition made). Then `root.updateWorldMatrix(false, false)` runs; this is the root's own
  half of the old call: the visual-ground `updateMatrix` with its time-dependent memo, plus the multiply,
  at the same point in the loop. Then the position is read from `matrixWorld.elements[12..14]`
  (`setFromMatrixPosition`).
- Any other root (a held item under a wielder's part, a detached root, a patched getWorldPosition) keeps
  the original call.

The chain nodes are plain Groups with no own `updateMatrix`, and nothing in the loop moves them, so
recomputing them once instead of N times leaves identical values and flags. Tested (§8 G): over 40 ticks
with entities near, far, crossing the 120 m radius, the far local player, a far jump-tween entity and a
held item, the same entities ticked and every root / ancestor / part matrix, matrixWorld and
`matrixWorldNeedsUpdate` matched before and after the walk.

## 7. Left on the JS path, and why

- **`tickEntityRenderVisibility` (FCULL).** Per entity it is a 6-plane sphere test and a distance test;
  the cost is JS object reads and `_occEntityBox`'s periodic `Box3.setFromObject` (a full three
  traversal that needs three's matrices). Rust has nothing to add without moving the matrices.
- **Visual-ground root matrices** (`visualGroundUpdateMatrix`). These are memoised. The memo re-reads
  wasm physics state on a cadence (`_readGravity`), so moving or skipping a call changes WHEN state is
  read, which would not be exact. The gate keeps every call where it was.
- **Mesh `matrixWorld` aliasing** — built as the opt-in `?rigMeshAlias` (§10). It is not exact BETWEEN
  walks, so it stays off until the owner decides.
- **Hoisting `performance.now()`** (dead-reckon staleness, material hooks) out of the loop would change
  borderline comparisons, so it was not done.

## 9. Risks / what to check first

1. **The Euler staleness.** Grep for any new `rotation.` use on rig parts, and for partial Euler writes in
   particular. A future AnimationMixer-style `.rotation` binding on parts would break.
2. **Descriptor lifetime.** Rust keeps a copy of every registered descriptor's arrays. They are released
   by the FinalizationRegistry when animation.js's cache lets the descriptor go, or by the 8 M-float cap
   (LRU by last pose). Watch `__rustRig.stats().floats` over a long session.
3. **A descriptor mutated in place** (a typed-array write into `partFrames` after build) would not be
   seen. Nothing does that today (builders only). Replacing the arrays IS detected and re-registers.
4. **scene_core `_resolve()` latches** on first use. If any module asked `sceneWasmClass` before
   index.html set `__hbSceneWasm`, every lane would stay on JS for the session. This bridge asks lazily,
   at the first pose.
5. **The gate** relies on entitiesGroup's ancestors never moving during a tick and having no own
   `updateMatrix`; both are true today (scene3d/index.js builds them once).
6. **`?rigMeshAlias`** (deleted 2026-10-30, §10). Its exactness holds at walks. Between walks a mesh's world follows its part
   (§10.4). Check first any NEW code that:
   - reads a rig mesh's `matrixWorld` without refreshing it, inside the frame;
   - writes a rig mesh's `matrixWorld` / `matrix` directly;
   - clones rig meshes;
   - moves part meshes without three's `remove` / `add`.

## 10. `?rigMeshAlias` — identity part meshes share their part's world matrix (opt-in, owner decision) — DELETED 2026-10-30

> **Deleted 2026-10-30 (round 3 R3-2).** On the 1070 the alias arm lost 7.5 / 11.5 / 3.3 fps (still / moving / tour) against the defaults (RC-BENCH v2 rep 1, docs/2026-10-29-round3-gpu-driven.md §1.1), so the code, its suite and its smoke were removed; the default (alias off) path is unchanged. Round 3's rig-side replacement is `?rigPoseSkip` (default OFF; skip a pose the rig already holds; tests/rig_pose_skip.test.mjs). This section, §1's row, §7's bullet, §8's test line and §9's risk 6 are kept as the record of what was built and measured.

### 10.1 What it does

A rig part's surface meshes sit at the part's origin, so three's walk computes each one as
`part.matrixWorld × I`. That is a compose of the identity into `mesh.matrix` and a 4×4 multiply written
into the mesh's own array, per mesh, every frame (2 of every 3 rig nodes).

Under `?rigMeshAlias=on`, every part built by `_spawnImpl` gets an own `updateMatrixWorld`
(scene3d/setup_rig.js `installRigMeshAlias`):
- For the part itself it runs three r184's body. A hidden part goes to three's skip_hidden-patched
  method, which alone knows whether this is a scene walk.
- For its children, an identity mesh shares the part's Matrix4 (`mesh.matrixWorld === part.matrixWorld`).
  Its matrixAutoUpdate and matrixWorldAutoUpdate are off, so neither three's walk nor `updateWorldMatrix`
  writes through it, and a walk costs only a re-validation.
- Every other child goes to its own `updateMatrixWorld` exactly as three's loop would call it.

### 10.2 Exactness at every walk

`P × I` (three's `multiplyMatrices`) equals `P` bit for bit when `P` holds no −0 and no ±Inf/NaN. The
×1 terms are exact and the +0 summands change nothing; a −0 entry can come out +0, and Inf × 0 is NaN.

So each walk checks the part's fresh world matrix (inlined, 16 compares). If it is not clean, its meshes
get their own matrices back for that frame and walk three's way. The mesh's local `matrix` is composed
once, from the exact identity, when it is aliased; three recomposes the same identity every frame.

Tests (`tests/rig_mesh_alias.test.mjs`) inject a −0 and a NaN into a world-frozen part to exercise this:

| Run | Coverage | Real diffs | Signed-zero-only diffs | Flag mismatches |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Synthetic worlds | 60 walks, 13,267 node comparisons | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| EntityManager A/B | 82 ticks | 0 | 0 | 0 |

Mesh-vs-product checks (`multiplyMatrices(parent.matrixWorld, mesh.matrix)`): 12,050.

### 10.3 Which meshes qualify, and what drops the alias

A mesh qualifies if it meets all of these:
- a plain `THREE.Mesh` (not skinned / instanced / batched) with no children;
- visible when first aliased;
- matrixAutoUpdate and matrixWorldAutoUpdate on, `pivot === null`;
- no own or class override of `updateMatrix` / `updateMatrixWorld` / `updateWorldMatrix`;
- an EXACT identity local transform: position (+0,+0,+0), quaternion (+0,+0,+0,1), scale (1,1,1).

A mesh is tested on the first walk that meets it. A rejected one (or one whose alias was dropped) is
re-tested on one walk in eight, staggered by index; it walks three's way meanwhile, which is exact.

Re-validated every walk, inline:
- position components `=== 0` (a −0 position still gives a bit-identical WORLD matrix when `P` is clean;
  only the unread local matrix would hold +0 where three composes −0);
- scale exactly 1, `pivot === null`, no children;
- the mesh's auto-update flags still off;
- `mesh.matrixWorld` still the part's object;
- the part's matrix is clean.

Hooks:
- The mesh's quaternion and Euler change callbacks are wrapped. Any rotation write drops the alias at
  the next walk: dismember's dislocation, `applyMatrix4`, `attach`'s decompose, a `rotation.set`.
- The part's `childremoved` event drops it at once, before anything can walk it elsewhere. That covers
  detach, reparent to another part or rig, `attach` to the entities group (debris), dismember's strip,
  the equip hot-swap, `clear()` and `bulk_child_remove`. Every mesh move in the app goes through three's
  `remove` / `add` [C].

Specials stay on three's path: InstancedMesh / SkinnedMesh / BatchedMesh, meshes with children, meshes
with own matrix methods, lights, cameras, held items (nested rig roots — their parts alias on their own),
drone props. `materials.js` wireframe-fill companions are created at spawn (before any walk), copy
`matrixAutoUpdate = true` and alias themselves.

Tested:
- poses, root moves;
- hides of meshes, parts and roots;
- a dislocation and its heal;
- reparents: part → part, rig → rig, attach to the entities group and back;
- strip + `restoreParts`, a mesh carried to another entity and back;
- the equip swap;
- scale / pivot / full-Euler / `applyMatrix4` writes, a flag flipped by "someone";
- skip-hidden off, direct `updateMatrixWorld` calls;
- the jump tween, a frozen corpse pose.

### 10.4 What a reader sees (the audit) — the behaviour differences

The alias changes WHEN a mesh's world matrix changes. Three writes it at walks (and when the mesh itself
is refreshed); aliased, it is the part's, so it also changes whenever the part is refreshed. Each reader:

| Reader | How it reads mesh.matrixWorld | With the alias |
|---|---|---|
| three's projectObject / renderObject / shadow maps | after the walk | identical |
| picking (`intersectObjects`, `pickBySphere`) | no refresh; runs between frames (DOM events / its own rAF) | identical (R1). After a mid-frame part-only refresh it would see the part's fresher pose (R2 shows the case is real); no picking runs inside the tick |
| `_occEntityBox` / carnage impact point / play_effect_vfx (`Box3.setFromObject`) | refreshes every node first | identical boxes (R3); ±0 only if a refresh left a −0 in `P` |
| lighting `_measureRigRadius`, shadow-only casters (`updateWorldMatrix(false, true)`), fx_ribbons blade, lifestone_fx | refresh first | identical (R4) |
| particle anchors / hooks (partFrames proxy), weapon_fx, nameplates (root), sort centers | read PARTS or roots | unaffected (R5) |
| blood decals, ragdoll env rays | statics / cells only | unaffected |
| film / drone | cameras, cells, statics, props under parts | unaffected |
| a HIDDEN aliased mesh | — | tracks its part where three leaves it at its last visible walk (6 mesh-frames in the S run). Only refreshing readers or hidden-hit-discarding raycasts look at it, so nothing observable changes |

Other effects:
- `Object3D.copy` / `clone` of an aliased mesh would copy its auto-update flags off (no code clones rig
  meshes).
- `__skipHiddenMatrix.census()` does not see the part subtrees this walks.
- `mesh.matrixWorld === part.matrixWorld`, so code that WROTE into a mesh's matrixWorld would write the
  part's. No such writer exists [C].

### 10.5 Measurements (node 20 / V8, laptop) [M]

Paired runs: per round, three's walk then the alias walk; median of 21 rounds; repeated in separate
processes. 100 rigs × 17 parts × 2 meshes (5,200 entity nodes, ~8% hidden and ~5% offset surfaces), real
`installRigMeshAlias`, skip_hidden installed, every third part re-posed each frame.

| Heap | three µs/walk | alias µs/walk | less |
|---|---|---|---|
| compact | 1,227 / 1,643 / 1,521 | 974 / 1,356 / 1,201 | 20.9% / 18.6% / 19.9% |
| scattered | 1,280 / 1,220 / 1,670 | 1,163 / 1,035 / 1,540 | 9.0% / 11.5% / 8.6% |

- **Projection reads.** A projectObject-shaped pass (frustum sphere + view depth + modelView multiply
  per drawn mesh) reads 15–21% less, because the meshes of a part read one shared array.
- **Validation cost.** The per-walk position / scale re-validation costs about half the walk saving.
  Without it, trusting the quaternion hook plus the audit, the walk saving was ~16–19% where it is
  ~6–8% with it in the same harness. It stays in, because a position-only or scale-only writer would
  otherwise go unseen; there is none today.
- **Projected 1070 effect [D].** The entity share of the 0.78 ms matrix walk is ~0.5 ms, so roughly
  0.05–0.10 ms/frame from the walk, plus whatever the projection / draw reads gain. projectObject's
  traversal and the sort themselves are unchanged. Measure on the 1070 before deciding.
